summary: This note, a Wikipedia-derived article on the party leaders of the U.S. House of Representatives, describes the role and functions of the House minority leader. It covers institutional duties, the minority leader's role as de facto leader of the opposition when the President and Congress share a party, and how leadership succession works after a party loses the House. It also gives historical context, including the position's 20th-century development and early informal opposition leaders such as James Madison.
one_line: Overview of the U.S. House minority leader's institutional duties, opposition role, and historical succession patterns among House party leaders.
key_facts: The House minority leader and the majority leader each name three Members to serve as Private Calendar objectors.
The minority leader is a member of the United States Capitol Preservation Commission and is traditionally a member of the House Office Building Commission.
Minority Leaders who prominently opposed the incumbent President have included Gerald Ford, Richard Gephardt, Nancy Pelosi, and John Boehner.
Nancy Pelosi ran successfully for Minority Leader in the 112th Congress after the Democrats lost control of the House in the 2010 elections.
When the Republicans gained the House majority after the 2010 elections, Eric Cantor succeeded Boehner as Majority Leader.
Tom DeLay generally overshadowed Speaker Dennis Hastert from 2003 to 2006, the most recent exception to the rule that the Speaker is the majority party's leader.

Starting with Republican Nicholas Longworth in 1925, majority leaders generally ascended directly to the Speakership upon the incumbent's retirement, through the Democrats' control of the House from 1931 to 1995.
Charles A. Halleck served as Republican House leader and Minority Leader from 1959 to 1965.
Dick Gephardt became the Democrats' House leader as Minority Leader after his party lost control in the 1994 midterm elections.
John Boehner was elected Speaker when the House reconvened in 2011, after serving as Republican House leader and Minority Leader from 2007 to 2011.
In 1998, after Speaker Newt Gingrich announced his resignation, Dennis Hastert won the Speakership over Majority Leader Dick Armey and Majority Whip Tom DeLay.

Some scholars suggest James Madison of Virginia informally functioned as the first 'minority leader' by leading opposition to Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton's fiscal policies in the First Congress.
The minority leader may use discharge petitions, which require 218 signatures, to force minority initiatives to the floor over majority leadership opposition.

When the White House is controlled by the House majority party, the minority leader takes a larger role in formulating alternatives to executive branch initiatives, as Gerald Ford did during Lyndon Johnson's administration.
